pathophysiology.summary: End-stage COPD causes severe breathlessness, frequent exacerbations and chronic respiratory failure despite maximal inhaled therapy. Supportive care targets breathlessness, anxiety and planning for deterioration.
keyMechanisms: Hyperinflation and gas-exchange failure cause breathlessness and hypoxaemia; some develop chronic hypercapnia.
Chronic hypoxaemia → pulmonary hypertension and cor pulmonale (STS).
Opioids reduce the sensation of breathlessness (NICE NG115).

physicalSigns: Cyanosis, oedema (cor pulmonale), cachexia, accessory muscle use.
redFlags: Persistent hypercapnia 2 weeks after an exacerbation — consider home NIV (STS)

pathophysiology.summary: Advanced dementia brings severe cognitive and functional decline, inability to communicate needs, swallowing difficulty and frailty. Progression is unpredictable, so palliative care should be offered from diagnosis (NICE NG97).
keyMechanisms: Neurodegeneration impairs memory, language and executive function; pain and discomfort may show only as behaviour change.
Swallowing difficulty causes aspiration and weight loss; tube feeding does not improve outcomes in severe dementia (NICE NG97).
Antipsychotics increase harm and can cause severe sensitivity reactions in Lewy body or Parkinson's dementia (NICE NG97).

Live attenuated vaccines (MMR, varicella, rotavirus, OPV, BCG) give long-lasting immunity but can harm the immunosuppressed.

pathophysiology.summary: CAP is acute infection of the lung parenchyma acquired outside hospital. Alveoli fill with inflammatory exudate, causing consolidation, impaired gas exchange and, in severe cases, sepsis and respiratory failure.
keyMechanisms: Organisms reach the alveoli (usually by micro-aspiration) and overwhelm local defences; the inflammatory exudate fills air spaces (consolidation).
Ventilation–perfusion mismatch from consolidated lung causes hypoxaemia and tachypnoea.
The systemic inflammatory response can progress to sepsis, septic shock and multi-organ failure.
Resistant organisms (MRSA, Pseudomonas) are more likely after recent hospitalisation and IV antibiotics or with prior respiratory isolation.
Viral infection (e.g. influenza) can coexist with bacterial infection.

symptoms: Cough, sputum, fever, rigors, breathlessness, pleuritic chest pain.
Confusion (a severity criterion).
physicalSigns: Fever (or hypothermia below 36 °C in severe disease), tachypnoea, tachycardia, hypoxia.
Focal crackles, bronchial breathing, dullness to percussion.
Confusion; hypotension.
redFlags: ATS major criteria: septic shock needing vasopressors, or respiratory failure needing mechanical ventilation — direct ICU admission

Three or more ATS minor criteria: RR 30 or more, PaO2/FiO2 250 or less, multilobar infiltrates, confusion, urea (BUN) 20 mg/dL or more (about 7 mmol/L), WBC below 4 × 10⁹/L, platelets below 100 × 10⁹/L, temperature below 36 °C, hypotension needing aggressive fluids
PSI class V (above 130 points): ICU

Subacute course, weight loss, upper-lobe or cavitary change; MOH protocol cautions against fluoroquinolones without excluding TB.

pathophysiology.summary: Generalised anxiety disorder (GAD) is an anxiety disorder in which a person has anxiety or significant worry, often repeated worry about many different issues, and may seek reassurance about physical symptoms. NICE CG113 does not define GAD by symptom count or duration; it advises assessment of distress and functional impairment as well as symptoms. This topic covers GAD in adults, not panic disorder.
keyMechanisms: Diagnosis should not rely solely on the number, severity and duration of symptoms; distress and functional impairment are also assessed (NICE CG113 Rec. 1.2.6).

Comorbid depressive or other anxiety disorder, substance misuse, medical conditions, past mental health disorders and past treatment response may have affected development, course and severity (NICE CG113 Rec. 1.2.7).
Substance misuse can be a complication of GAD; harmful and dependent misuse should be treated first (NICE CG113 Rec. 1.2.9).
Some physical symptoms in people who attend primary care frequently may be due to GAD (NICE CG113 Recs 1.2.4–1.2.5).
CG113 does not describe the neurobiology of GAD.

clinicalManagement.title: Step 1: identify, assess, educate and monitor
actions: Be alert to anxiety disorders, especially with past anxiety disorder, somatic symptoms or recent trauma; consider the GAD-2 (NICE CG113 Rec. 1.2.2).
Identify and communicate the diagnosis early (NICE CG113 Rec. 1.2.3).
Do a full assessment covering distress, functional impairment, comorbidity, substance use and past treatments (NICE CG113 Recs 1.2.6–1.2.7).
Treat a more severe comorbid depressive or anxiety disorder first, and harmful or dependent substance misuse first (NICE CG113 Recs 1.2.8–1.2.9).
Give education about GAD and treatment options and actively monitor symptoms and functioning, which may improve less severe presentations (NICE CG113 Rec. 1.2.10).
Discuss over-the-counter medicines and their interaction risks (NICE CG113 Rec. 1.2.11).

clinicalManagement.title: Step 2: low-intensity psychological intervention
actions: Offer one or more of individual non-facilitated self-help, individual guided self-help or psychoeducational groups, guided by preference (NICE CG113 Rec. 1.2.12).
Non-facilitated self-help: CBT-based materials worked through over at least 6 weeks with minimal contact (NICE CG113 Rec. 1.2.13).
Guided self-help: CBT-based, usually 5 to 7 weekly or fortnightly sessions of 20 to 30 minutes (NICE CG113 Rec. 1.2.14).
Psychoeducational groups: usually 6 weekly 2-hour sessions with about 12 participants per therapist (NICE CG113 Rec. 1.2.15).

clinicalManagement.title: Step 3: high-intensity psychological treatment or drug treatment
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Marked impairment or inadequate response to step 2
actions: Offer either an individual high-intensity psychological intervention or drug treatment, explaining benefits and drawbacks including side effects and withdrawal; base the choice on preference (NICE CG113 Rec. 1.2.17).
Check for risk and comorbidity at each review and consider step 4 if criteria are met (NICE CG113 Rec. 1.2.37).
Offer CBT or applied relaxation, usually 12 to 15 weekly sessions of 1 hour (NICE CG113 Recs 1.2.18–1.2.20).
Offer an SSRI; consider sertraline first as most cost-effective, noting its off-label use for GAD in the UK at publication, with documented informed consent (NICE CG113 Rec. 1.2.23).

If sertraline is ineffective, offer another SSRI or an SNRI, weighing withdrawal tendency (paroxetine, venlafaxine), side effects, interactions, suicide risk and overdose toxicity (especially venlafaxine) and prior experience (NICE CG113 Rec. 1.2.24).
If SSRIs and SNRIs are not tolerated, consider pregabalin after assessing for a history of drug abuse (NICE CG113 Rec. 1.2.25).
Do not offer a benzodiazepine except as a short-term measure in crises, and do not offer an antipsychotic in primary care (NICE CG113 Recs 1.2.26–1.2.27).

pathophysiology.summary: Persistent high blood pressure damages the heart, brain, kidneys and eyes; target organ damage includes left ventricular hypertrophy, chronic kidney disease, hypertensive retinopathy and raised urine albumin:creatinine ratio (NG136, terms used). Benefit of treatment rises with absolute risk, so stage 1 hypertension is treated when target organ damage, cardiovascular disease, renal disease, diabetes or a 10-year cardiovascular risk of 10% or more is present (NG136 1.4.10). Drugs from different classes add together, so an ACE inhibitor or ARB, a calcium-channel blocker and a thiazide-like diuretic are combined in steps (NG136 1.4.41–1.4.45). Resistant hypertension is uncontrolled pressure on optimal doses of three drugs; it needs adherence checks and out-of-clinic confirmation before a fourth drug (NG136 1.4.46–1.4.48).

symptoms: Dizziness or falls after starting or changing drugs suggest postural hypotension (NG136 1.1.5).

physicalSigns: Clinic blood pressure 140/90 mmHg or higher: take a second reading and record the lower of the last two (NG136 1.2.2).
Arm difference above 15 mmHg on repeat: use the higher arm (NG136 1.2.1).

Retinal haemorrhage or papilloedema (NG136 1.5.2).
redFlags: Clinic pressure 180/120 mmHg or higher with retinal haemorrhage or papilloedema, new confusion, chest pain, signs of heart failure or acute kidney injury: same-day specialist assessment (NG136 1.5.2).
Suspected phaeochromocytoma: same-day specialist assessment (NG136 1.5.3).
Clinic pressure 180/120 mmHg or higher without those features: test for target organ damage as soon as possible and confirm within 7 days (NG136 1.5.1).
Age under 40 with hypertension: consider specialist evaluation for secondary causes (NG136 1.4.14).
precipitants: Excess alcohol, caffeine and high sodium intake (NG136 1.4.3–1.4.5).
White-coat effect: clinic pressure more than 20/10 mmHg above average daytime ABPM or HBPM (NG136, terms used).
Masked hypertension: normal clinic pressure but raised ABPM or HBPM (NG136, terms used).

clinicalManagement.title: Same-day referral check
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Every visit with pressure 180/120 mmHg or higher
actions: Refer the same day for retinal haemorrhage or papilloedema, new confusion, chest pain, signs of heart failure, acute kidney injury or suspected phaeochromocytoma (NG136 1.5.2–1.5.3).

Without those features, check target organ damage as soon as possible; if present consider starting drugs at once; if absent repeat pressure within 7 days or use ABPM or HBPM with review within 7 days (NG136 1.5.1).

clinicalManagement.title: Decide whether to start drugs
actions: Offer drugs with lifestyle advice for persistent stage 2 hypertension at any age (NG136 1.4.9).

Discuss drugs for stage 1 under 80 with target organ damage, cardiovascular disease, renal disease, diabetes or 10-year risk of 10% or more; consider for under 60 with risk below 10%; consider over 80 if clinic pressure is above 150/90 mmHg (NG136 1.4.10, 1.4.12–1.4.13).
Explain individual risk and the option of no treatment; keep offering lifestyle advice either way (NG136 1.4.11).

clinicalManagement.title: Step 1
actions: Prefer once-daily drugs and non-proprietary products (NG136 1.4.26–1.4.27). Never combine an ACE inhibitor with an ARB (NG136 1.4.34).
If starting or changing a diuretic, prefer a thiazide-like diuretic such as indapamide (NG136 1.4.38).

branches.condition: Type 2 diabetes at any age, or under 55 and not of Black African or African-Caribbean origin
actions: ACE inhibitor or ARB; ARB if the ACE inhibitor is not tolerated, for example cough (NG136 1.4.32–1.4.33).

branches.condition: Aged 55 or over without type 2 diabetes, or Black African or African-Caribbean origin without type 2 diabetes
actions: Calcium-channel blocker; thiazide-like diuretic if it is not tolerated, for example oedema (NG136 1.4.35–1.4.36). For Black African or African-Caribbean origin consider an ARB in preference to an ACE inhibitor (NG136 1.4.30).
Thiazide-like diuretic and follow the chronic heart failure guideline (NG136 1.4.37).

clinicalManagement.title: Step 2
actions: Check the person takes the medicine as prescribed and support adherence before adding a drug (NG136 1.4.40).
On an ACE inhibitor or ARB add a calcium-channel blocker or a thiazide-like diuretic (NG136 1.4.41).
On a calcium-channel blocker add an ACE inhibitor, an ARB or a thiazide-like diuretic (NG136 1.4.42).

clinicalManagement.title: Step 3
actions: Review doses (optimal tolerated) and adherence (NG136 1.4.44).
Combine an ACE inhibitor or ARB, a calcium-channel blocker and a thiazide-like diuretic (NG136 1.4.45).

clinicalManagement.title: Resistant hypertension (step 4)
clinicalManagement.timeframe: If not controlled on optimal step 3
actions: Confirm with ABPM or HBPM, assess postural hypotension and discuss adherence before adding anything (NG136 1.4.47).
Potassium 4.5 mmol/L or less: consider low-dose spironolactone (off-label use at March 2019); take care when eGFR is reduced (NG136 1.4.49).
Potassium above 4.5 mmol/L: consider an alpha-blocker or beta-blocker (NG136 1.4.51).
Monitor sodium, potassium and renal function within 1 month of starting a further diuretic (NG136 1.4.50).
Still uncontrolled on four optimal drugs: seek specialist advice (NG136 1.4.52).

clinicalManagement.title: Monitor against the target
actions: Use clinic pressure to monitor response; same targets with or without cardiovascular disease (NG136 1.4.15, 1.4.23).

Target: clinic below 140/90 mmHg under 80 and below 150/90 mmHg at 80 or over; ABPM or HBPM below 135/85 mmHg under 80 and below 145/85 mmHg at 80 or over; use clinical judgement in frailty or multimorbidity (NG136 1.4.20–1.4.22).
Check postural pressure in type 2 diabetes, with symptoms, and at 80 or over (NG136 1.4.16). Advise HBPM for self-monitoring and train the person (NG136 1.4.17, 1.4.19).
Give an annual review of pressure, support, lifestyle, symptoms and medicines (NG136 1.4.24).

pathophysiology.summary: Intrapartum fetal compromise is hypoxia developing during labour, when contractions intermittently reduce placental blood flow. A healthy fetus tolerates this; a fetus with reduced reserve, or one exposed to excessive contractions, cord compression or acute events, can become acidotic.
keyMechanisms: Each contraction transiently reduces uteroplacental flow; too-frequent contractions (5 or more in 10 minutes or hypertonus) shorten recovery time (NICE).
Cord compression causes variable decelerations; uteroplacental insufficiency causes late decelerations.
Developing hypoxia or infection raises the baseline heart rate; worsening hypoxia reduces variability (NICE).
Acute events — cord prolapse, abruption, uterine rupture — cause sudden bradycardia.

symptoms: Often none; meconium-stained liquor, fever, bleeding, abdominal pain or slow progress raise concern (NICE lists slow progress, sepsis, meconium).
physicalSigns: Fetal heart abnormalities on auscultation or CTG.
Maternal tachycardia, fever, hypotension; abnormal uterine tone.
redFlags: Acute bradycardia or a single prolonged deceleration of 3 minutes or more

No acceleration after fetal scalp stimulation

Do not give maternal facial oxygen for fetal concerns; do not use amnioinfusion (NICE).

Second stage: obstetric review; consider stopping pushing and oxytocin unless birth is imminent.

pathophysiology.summary: End-of-life breathlessness and pain are distressing symptoms with mixed causes — disease progression, complications (effusion, pulmonary oedema, infection, fracture) and anxiety. Opioids reduce both the perception of breathlessness and pain.
keyMechanisms: Breathlessness arises from increased respiratory drive, mechanical load (effusion, ascites), hypoxaemia and anxiety.
Opioids reduce respiratory drive and the sensation of breathlessness; benzodiazepines relieve associated anxiety (NICE NG31).
Oxygen helps only when hypoxaemia is present (NICE NG31 1.5.16).
Pain may come from tumour, bone, nerves or reversible causes such as urinary retention (NICE NG31 1.5.11).

physicalSigns: Tachypnoea, accessory muscle use; signs of effusion, pulmonary oedema or infection.
SpO2 if it would change care; pain behaviours using a validated tool when communication is limited.

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Crackles, orthopnoea; diuretic may relieve.

pathophysiology.summary: Tobacco dependence is a chronic relapsing condition driven by nicotine. Tobacco smoke causes cancer, cardiovascular and respiratory disease; stopping at any age reduces risk.
keyMechanisms: Nicotine acts on brain nicotinic receptors → dopamine release → reinforcement and withdrawal on stopping.
Varenicline is a partial agonist that reduces craving and the reward of smoking.
Combined short- and long-acting NRT, or varenicline, with behavioural support are most effective (NICE NG209).

clinicalManagement.title: Ask and advise
actions: Record status; give clear advice to stop; offer support (PHA, NICE NG209).

clinicalManagement.title: Treat
actions: Offer behavioural support to everyone (NICE NG209).
Most effective with support: combination short- and long-acting NRT, or varenicline (NICE NG209). Cytisinicline and bupropion are other options; not under 18.
Varenicline: 0.5 mg once daily days 1–3, 0.5 mg twice daily days 4–7, then 1 mg twice daily for 12 weeks (label); set quit date or quit between days 8 and 35.
Prescribe before the quit date (NICE NG209).

actions: Review progress, side effects and relapse; another 12 weeks of varenicline may be added for those who stopped (label).
